tier_reason: Upgraded B to A. DRMacIver/rust-bigint-benchmarks is a third-party suite (written for dashu) with public criterion code in benches/primitive.rs, small_int.rs, workload.rs and shrinker.rs, run against rug/GMP with --features gmp. The report states rustc 1.92.0 and an Apple M2 Max. The flags are Cargo's default bench profile (opt-level=3): Cargo.toml has no [profile] override, and the repo has no .cargo/config or rust-toolchain file. Cargo.lock pins malachite-nz 0.9.1, rug 1.30.0 and gmp-mpfr-sys 1.7.1.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Tiny operands and parsing only, on an Apple M2 Max against rug 1.30.0 (GMP). At 10 bits: ubig_add malachite 2.1 ns vs rug 17.7 ns, ubig_mul 3.0 ns vs 18.0 ns, ubig_gcd 8.5 ns vs 20.9 ns, ubig_gcd_ext 25.8 ns vs 53.7 ns, ubig_pow 5.1 ns vs 41.6 ns, ubig_to_dec 10.1 ns vs 37.5 ns. Decimal and hex parsing beat rug at every size: ubig_from_dec at 10^4 bits 8.37 us vs 11.51 us, ubig_from_hex at 10^4 bits 3.13 us vs 6.60 us; string_round_trip 1.80 ms vs 1.97 ms. From about 100 to 1000 bits up, rug wins: ubig_mul at 10^4 bits malachite 8.28 us vs rug 4.52 us, ubig_gcd_ext at 1000 bits 3.40 us vs 3.18 us, ubig_modulo_pow at 10^4 bits 250.90 ms vs 143.02 ms.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.92.0 (ded5c06cf 2025-12-08); cargo bench --features gmp with Cargo's default bench profile (opt-level=3; no [profile] override, no .cargo/config); criterion 0.5.1, 1 s warm-up, 2 s measurement, 100 samples; malachite-nz 0.9.1, rug 1.30.0 via gmp-mpfr-sys 1.7.1 (Cargo.lock); the GMP build (bundled or system) is not stated
corrections.caveats: Malachite beats GMP only on one- and two-word integers, where GMP's per-value allocation dominates, and on decimal/hex parsing. The same report counts malachite fastest in 27 of 205 cases and rug in 52, with rug ahead on add, sub, mul, div, gcd, pow and modular arithmetic from about 100 to 1000 bits up. The second suite (github.com/tczajka/bigint-benchmark-rs, malachite 0.4.14 vs rug 1.24.1) has rug faster on every task: digits of e at 10M, rug 2.788 s vs malachite 3.689 s; Fibonacci at 100M, rug 2.937 s vs malachite 5.192 s. The report calls itself 'quick, machine-specific local numbers, not authoritative' and uses a short criterion measurement time. It benchmarks malachite-nz 0.9.1, while the repo is now at 0.12.0. Malachite's own site (malachite.rs) is blocked from this container, so no first-party claim was recorded. The library is pure Rust with no C/C++ API.

notes: Numbers match the report exactly. The baseline is rug (the Rust wrapper of GMP), so the tiny-operand wins partly reflect rug/mpz allocation overhead rather than GMP's kernels. Repo is active (last commit 2026-09-30) with 586 stars; malachite-nz/Cargo.toml declares LGPL-3.0-only, and the workspace is now at 0.12.0.

tier_reason: Upgraded C to A. The benchmark code is public: tests/benchmark/blip_mp_bench.zig and tests/benchmark/gmp_bench.c, built by build.zig's bench step and flake.nix packages.bench. Zig 0.16.0 is used with -Doptimize=ReleaseFast, and the GMP harness is compiled with -O3. nixpkgs is pinned in flake.lock (rev 1c3fe55a), which fixes the GMP build, plus a --disable-assembly variant. RESULTS.md and BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md Run 17 name the CPU as an Apple M4, and Run 18 names an AMD Ryzen 9 7940HS. The numbers are first-party 3-run hand medians, and the README overstates some of them (see claimed_speedup).

corrections.hardware: Apple M4, aarch64-darwin (stated in RESULTS.md and BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md Run 17); cross-check on an AMD Ryzen 9 7940HS (Zen 4) Framework laptop under NixOS (BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md Run 18)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0, zig build bench -Doptimize=ReleaseFast (tests/benchmark/blip_mp_bench.zig); GMP harness tests/benchmark/gmp_bench.c compiled with -O3 -Wall -Wextra and linked against nixpkgs GMP (nixos-unstable pinned in flake.lock rev 1c3fe55a) and against a --disable-assembly GMP override; libc malloc on both sides; run via nix build .#bench; 3-run hand medians
corrections.claimed_speedup: Apple M4 vs GMP with assembly, from RESULTS.md. All i64-fitting adds are 1.95-2.66x faster (RESULTS.md: immediate add 2.06 ns vs 4.83 ns, 2.34x). Mul: 12 of 15 sizes from 128 to 8192 bits are faster, including RSA-1024 1.20x (210 vs 252 ns), RSA-2048 1.19x (673 vs 800 ns), RSA-3072 1.37x (1265 vs 1733 ns) and 1536 bits 1.45x; 16384 bits is 0.87x and 32768 bits 0.55x. Sub is 1.03-2.11x faster from 256 to 8192 bits (768 bits: 4.38 vs 9.23 ns). Add is 1.04-1.28x faster at 768 bits and above. powm is 13% faster at 2048 bits (3333 vs 3839 us), 3% at 1024 and 8% at 3072. The public Mp.divMod is 1.25-2.00x SLOWER than mpz_tdiv_qr from 256 to 8192 bits (2048: 526.7 vs 416.5 ns). The README's 'divMod 1.31x' is blip vs GMP-noasm on x86 (452.8 vs 593.2 ns), and its '24% faster long division' is a limb-only inner kernel (~470 vs 614 ns). invMod is 3.25-5.36x slower. On Zen 4 vs GMP with assembly, only i64-fitting adds win (immediate add 3.36 vs 4.44 ns); mul at 2048-32768 bits loses by 2.24-3.36x, powm at 2048 by 1.99x and divMod at 2048 by 2.09x.
corrections.caveats: First-party 3-run hand medians, and the author lists hyperfine aggregation as to-do. The README headline mixes runs and machines. Its RSA-2048 'trifecta' divMod win (1.31x) is not supported on Apple Silicon, where RESULTS.md's own table shows the full divMod 1.26x slower. The '24% faster' long-division figure is an inner-kernel microbenchmark against a GMP timing (614 ns) about 1.5x higher than the 400-417 ns mpz_tdiv_qr timings in other tables. The README's 'honest losses' list (128-256-bit mul 0.40-0.67x) is stale against RESULTS.md (128-bit mul 1.38x faster). BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md Run 17's sub table has raw timings that contradict its ratios (256 bits: 6.87 ns vs 5.49 ns is marked a 1.28x win). Cross-check counts differ between documents (8240, 12029, 13029). The wins are Apple Silicon only: on Zen 4, GMP's assembly is 1.65-3.88x faster than GMP-noasm, and blip_mp loses every tier-3 size to it by 1.5-4x. Modular inverse is 2.5-5x slower than GMP. There is no LICENSE file; the README says 'MIT or Apache-2.0 (TBD before tagging a release)', so usability is reference. The repo has 1 star, the project is research-grade, and the benchmark runs are dated 2026-05-02 to 2026-05-04.

notes: Real entry with a reproducible harness, so the tier rises to A. The claim was overstated, though: drop the divMod win and treat 'long division 24% faster' as an inner-kernel-only result; this is worth recording as a shortcoming. License null and usability reference are confirmed (LICENSE, LICENSE-MIT, LICENSE-APACHE, LICENSE.md and COPYING all 404, and none is in the root listing). Last commit 2026-09-27, 1 star, active.

tier_reason: The README speed-up table (V100 vs a 20-core Xeon E5-2698v4 running GMP 6.1.2 with OpenMP) is first-party. The harness is public (perf_tests/xmp_tester.cu, perf_tests/gmp_tester.cc and the gmp-run targets). Neither the nvcc/CUDA nor the g++ version is stated, and the GMP harness Makefile line has no optimisation flag, so this falls short of A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: perf_tests/Makefile: nvcc -I../include -arch=sm_70 xmp_tester.cu -lgmp (no explicit -O; CUDA 10+ required for Volta, exact version not stated); GMP side: g++ gmp_tester.cc -o gmp_tester -lgmp -fopenmp (no -O flag, so the harness loop builds at g++'s default -O0; libgmp itself is built separately with its own ./configure); compiler versions and GMP configure flags not stated
corrections.caveats: Numbers are first-party, from the 2018 beta on a V100 against GMP 6.1.2 (current GMP is 6.3.x). This compares a GPU with a CPU, so it measures per-device throughput on large batches of independent operations, not a better algorithm; single-operand latency would lose to GMP. The GMP driver (perf_tests/gmp_tester.cc) is compiled with no optimisation flag, which inflates loop overhead around the cheapest calls and probably the 128-bit add/sub ratios (174x). Only libgmp's own code is optimised. Compiler versions are not stated. A third-party report (pscamillo/mr_blackwell README) says CGBN runs 'orders of magnitude slower than expected' on Blackwell (sm_120) GPUs, and the Makefile lists architectures only up to Ampere. steleman/nvidia-cgbn is a fork adding signed integers and Ada/Blackwell support (tested with CUDA 12.9/13.2); it is not reported separately. Supports fixed sizes only, up to 32K bits in multiples of 32.

notes: The README table matches the record exactly. The LICENSE file is the MIT text (Copyright 2015 NVIDIA), with 252 stars, 80 forks, last commit 2026-03-31, not archived and not a fork. The prime-gap usage is confirmed: sethtroisi/prime-gap README says gap_test_gpu is experimental and uses CGBN.
